blindSummary:
This country is safe in practice but thin in law for transgender visitors. Hate crimes and hate speech based on sexual orientation are penalised, and discrimination on grounds including gender identity is banned. There is no functioning legal gender recognition process (a regional LGBTI-rights index lists this country among states without one), but that is a resident-facing gap: a visitor faces no legal exposure whatsoever. It is a very small, heavily-policed, very low-crime tourist enclave embedded in a larger neighbouring country; street violence of any kind is rare.

No bathroom laws, no border friction (entry is through the neighbouring country's common visa rules), no documented anti-trans incidents. The overall picture reflects the gap between de facto safety (very high) and legal thinness (no legal gender recognition, limited explicit trans protections). Assessment caveat: very small jurisdiction with limited data. Single incidents and absent documentation carry correspondingly little evidential weight; do not over-interpret sparse data in either direction.
blindOutOfScope: Family-law gaps (no marriage equality, cohabitation contracts only) are resident-facing.
blindSourceSummaries: An international LGBT-rights organisation's country overview (updated March 2026): same-sex intimacy legal but very few protections - cohabitation agreements only (no marriage or adoption); hate crimes and hate speech on sexual orientation penalised; no SOGISC discrimination ban; no legal procedure for name/gender change, though in 2022 a trans person changed markers via an affirmative court decision for the first time; no nonbinary recognition; intersex genital mutilation not banned; no official Pride; limited visibility.
A country page on a regional LGBTI legal-equality index: this country's overall score and per-category compliance breakdown.
LGBT travel-guide site: a gay travel guide for this country - LGBT-friendly accommodation and destination information for the microstate.

A foreign government's 2023 human-rights report on this country: no significant changes; significant issues limited to libel laws and laws criminalising insult of the head of state (not enforced); no torture, arbitrary detention or other abuses reported.

Regional daily, via this country's human-rights commission (March 2025): a feature on the everyday legal challenges faced by LGBT people here - inheritance, filiation, parental leave and nationality; homosexuality decriminalised since the 18th century, yet this country ranks near the bottom of its region's LGBT-rights rankings; no equal succession, survivor pensions or parental leave; only ~10 people dare be out; a rapporteur for a regional human-rights body summed the record up as dismal.
An LGBT travel site's country guide: 'LGBT rights in this country: everything you should know before you visit' - covering the legal situation and travel considerations.
blindLocalsOnly: The absence of any legal gender recognition process is resident-facing.
